nameStory: The Ilia Underwing gets its name from the beautiful hidden 'underwings' — bright orange to deep red hindwings that are concealed beneath camouflaged forewings when at rest. The specific name 'ilia' comes from the Roman name Ilia, another name for Rhea Silvia, the legendary mother of Romulus and Remus in Roman mythology. It's also called the 'beloved underwing' or 'wife underwing,' perhaps referring to the moth's striking beauty when it reveals its colorful hidden wings.
description: The Ilia Underwing is a medium-to-large moth with a wingspan of about 2.5 to 3.2 inches across. When resting with wings folded, it looks like a piece of tree bark with mottled gray and brown forewings that provide perfect camouflage. The real show happens when it flies or is startled — flashing brilliant orange to deep red hindwings (the 'underwings') that can startle predators. These moths are active at night and are often attracted to lights during summer months.

idTips.label: White-circled spot
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive white circle on the forewing that encompasses a darker spot — this is the most reliable identifying feature that separates Ilia from other underwing moths

idTips.label: Orange to red underwings
idTips.description: The hindwings flash bright orange to deep red when the moth flies or opens its wings, ranging from pale peachy-orange to rich brick red

idTips.label: Bark-like forewings
idTips.description: The forewings feel papery and have a complex pattern of grays, browns, and mottled markings that perfectly mimic tree bark texture when viewed up close

idTips.label: Size and wingspan
idTips.description: These are substantial moths — about the size of your palm when wings are spread, with a solid, robust body that feels surprisingly heavy if handled

idTips.label: Variable forewing patterns
idTips.description: The camouflage pattern on the forewings can vary dramatically between individuals, from light gray-brown to dark charcoal, but always with intricate wavy lines

habitat: Look for Ilia Underwings in oak forests and mixed woodlands throughout New England, especially areas with black, red, white, or bur oaks where their caterpillars feed. They prefer mature forest edges, parks with large oak trees, and suburban areas with established oak populations. Adults are commonly attracted to outdoor lights, porch lights, and moth sheets near wooded areas during summer nights.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active yet, but look for young caterpillars beginning to feed on emerging oak leaves in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season from June through August — adults are active at night and readily come to lights, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flight season continues into September, with late-emerging adults still active on warm nights, while caterpillars are completing their development on oak trees.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not present — the species overwinters as eggs laid on oak bark, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: Ilia Underwings are masters of psychological warfare — when threatened, they suddenly flash their bright underwings while making erratic flight patterns, creating a startling 'now you see it, now you don't' effect that can confuse bats and birds just long enough for the moth to escape to safety.
confusionNotes: Ilia Underwings are easily confused with other underwing moth species, especially the Ultronia Underwing, but the distinctive white circle around a spot on the forewing is unique to Ilia. Memory trick: 'Ilia has a white ring like a wedding ring' — referring to its alternate name 'wife underwing.'
contextualKnowledge: The underwing moths (Catocala species) are sometimes called 'sweetheart moths' by collectors, and there are dozens of species in North America. The naming can be confusing because many have multiple common names — Ilia is also called beloved underwing or wife underwing interchangeably.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Ultronia Underwing, the Ilia has that diagnostic white circle on the forewing that Ultronia lacks. Both species have similar orange-red underwings and bark-like camouflage, but Ultronia tends to have more contrasting black and white markings on the forewings without the distinctive white-circled spot. Both are attracted to the same oak trees and lights, making the white circle the key field mark.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the Ilia Underwing, the Ultronia has distinctly darker, more wine-red hindwings rather than the bright orange-red of its cousin.
